transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess since I stopped working, I’ve had a hard time just… slowing down. It’s not terrible or anything, I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but I’m up and moving all day, going from one little job to the next around the house, almost like I still have a crew waiting on me to get things done. I figured maybe it was worth asking about, if that makes sense.
Would you say this need to stay busy and keep things in order has always been part of who you are, or is this something new that started around the time you stopped working?

I’ve probably always liked having something to do, sure, but it didn’t really feel like a problem until after I retired from handyman work. That was… about a year and two months ago now, I think. Since then it’s been harder to just sit still and leave things be, if that answers it right.

Has this drive to stay busy and keep things orderly caused any friction with your family or affected your relationships or daily life, or does it mainly just keep you occupied without causing problems?

It’s mostly just kept me occupied, I’d like to say… but, well, there have been a few bumps. My wife has kind of had to take over the calendar for us and check behind me on things, which I don’t love admitting. And I’ve had to apologize more than once to folks at the community center and the garden group for dropping the ball or letting people down. Nothing awful, I hope, but enough that it’s noticeable, I guess.

Before you retired, would people who knew you well—like coworkers, friends, or family—have described you as someone who was very perfectionistic, rigid about rules, or overly focused on order and control in most areas of your life, even back in your 20s and 30s?

I’m not sure I’d say that, no. I mean, I liked things done right, like most people do, especially on a job, but I don’t know that folks would’ve called me rigid or controlling. At least, I don’t think so. My family might have their own wording, I suppose, but I wouldn’t want to overstate it.
Since you retired, have you been feeling noticeably more anxious, worried, or down about this change, beyond just having trouble sitting still?

I don’t know that I’d call it anxious or down, exactly. I mean, retirement’s been an adjustment, sure, but I wouldn’t want to make it sound worse than it is. Mostly it’s just… I notice I do better when I’ve got something to do. I haven’t really thought of myself as worried or depressed, if that’s what you mean.
Since it's been about 14 months since you stopped working, would you say this restlessness and need to stay busy has gotten better, stayed the same, or gotten worse over that time?

I’d say it really became noticeable after I stopped doing handyman work, so… about a year and two months ago now. I kept thinking it would settle once I got used to being retired, but it’s still been there. Not terrible, I don’t want to overstate it, but that’s when it turned into more of a real problem.
Do you find it hard to let others help with tasks or chores unless they do things exactly your way, even now in retirement?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I have my preferences for how things get done, like anybody, but I’m usually glad if someone helps. I might notice if it’s not how I’d do it, but I don’t think I make a big issue of it. At least I hope not.

Since retiring, when you do take time to relax or do something purely for fun, how does that feel to you—are you able to enjoy it, or do you feel guilty or restless until you get back to being productive?

I can enjoy it some, I guess, but it’s hard for me to really settle into it. I don’t know that I’d say “guilty” exactly… it’s more like I start feeling like I ought to be up doing something.

Since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down much. I’ll go from one little job to the next all day, like there’s still a crew waiting on me or something. Maybe that sounds silly, but sitting just for fun doesn’t come real easy.
Would you say this constant need to stay busy is genuinely distressing to you emotionally, or is it more just an inconvenience that hasn't really gotten you down?

It’s probably more than just an inconvenience, if I’m being honest. I don’t want to make it sound dramatic, but it does bother me that I can’t seem to slow down.

Since I stopped working, I’m up and moving from one little job to the next all day, like I still have a crew waiting on me. It wears on me some, emotionally, I guess… mostly because I feel like I should be able to relax now, and I can’t quite do it.
Since you retired, have you noticed yourself feeling sad, down, or low in spirits on most days, even when you're staying busy?
I don’t think I’d say sad most days, no. I mean, I get frustrated with myself sometimes, but low in spirits… not really. At least not that I’ve noticed in that way. Does that make sense?

Would you say the way this has affected you feels like more than what most people would typically go through when adjusting to retirement, or does it feel like a fairly normal, expected reaction to such a big life change?

I’d like to say it’s just normal retirement stuff, and maybe some of it is. But… I guess it has caused more trouble than I’d want to admit.

My wife’s had to pretty much take over keeping the calendar and checking behind me, because I’ll miss things or get mixed up. And I’ve had to apologize more than once to folks at the community center and the garden group for letting them down.

So, I don’t know… maybe that’s more than the usual adjustment? I don’t want to make too much of it, but it has affected other people, not just me.

Aside from feeling like you need to stay busy, do you also notice things like nervous tension, worry that won't quiet down, or physical restlessness in your body—like a racing heart or muscle tension?

Not so much a racing heart or anything like that, at least I don’t think so. But physically restless, yes… a bit.

Like if I’m sitting through a quiet meeting, or a church talk, I’ll feel like I need to shift around or tap my foot. Sometimes I’m thinking, “I should just get up and stretch,” even though I know I’m supposed to sit still. I try not to make a nuisance of myself, but it’s there.
Before you retired, were you able to relax and enjoy downtime without this same restless, need-to-be-productive feeling, or has some version of this always been there?

I think some version of it was probably always there, but work sort of gave it a place to go, if that makes sense. I had a reason to be moving and checking on things.

Since I stopped working, that’s when I really noticed I can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and down all day, going from one little job to the next like there’s still a crew waiting on me or something. I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is, but relaxing doesn’t come too easy right now.

Maybe a little, but I wouldn’t want to overstate it. It’s mostly that even at the end of the day, I still feel like I should be doing one more thing.

I don’t know if that’s the kind of thing you mean with sleep, but it can make it harder to settle down.

A little, yes… I mean, I’m still getting by, so I don’t want to make it sound like I can’t manage things. But it has happened more than I’d like.

I’ve forgotten to return calls from the community center, and there was a bill I didn’t pay until my wife reminded me. And once or twice I said I’d bring supplies for the garden group and then walked out without them.

It’s embarrassing to say, because I don’t want it to sound like I’m careless. It’s just… lately those things slip past me more than they used to.
